title: To UDL or Not to UDL? I Have Questions
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Haili Hughes examines Universal Design for Learning, the CAST framework built on multiple means of engagement, representation, and action and expression, from the perspective of a teacher already stretched by workload. She credits UDL with pushing schools and universities to take accessibility seriously and moving away from deficit models of SEND, but questions whether it is a coherent model at all, since studies label very different interventions as UDL and so cannot show which component produced any effect. She reviews the evidence, noting a moderate positive meta-analytic effect alongside a small, heterogeneous base reliant on weak designs, and highlights Guy Boysen's 2024 critique finding that much cited research did not test UDL as a framework or even measure learning. She warns that poorly understood UDL can drift toward learning-styles thinking, that more choice can raise extraneous load, and that the mode of expression is sometimes the learning goal itself. She prefers formative assessment and responsive teaching, keeping the learning goal stable while removing only difficulties irrelevant to what pupils are meant to learn.
points: Hughes argues that asking questions about the evidence for UDL is part of being evidence-informed, not a rejection of inclusion.
Because many different interventions are all labelled UDL, positive findings cannot tell teachers which practice to adopt tomorrow morning.
She cites Boysen's analysis that CAST's supporting studies often did not test UDL, offer real choice, or measure learning, and that evidence for individual techniques does not validate the framework.
Offering more choice may increase extraneous cognitive load, and when the goal is a sustained written argument a poster or podcast cannot stand in for the essay.
She prefers responsive teaching that detects barriers as learning unfolds over pre-emptively anticipating every barrier, which she sees as a risk to expectations and equity.
quotes: That is the thing I am interested in - not the high fallutin’ abstract research, but what impact it has on the actual teachers, doing the work. I think, when you are not doing the work, it is easy to have some halycon vision of teachers providing 3 different activities, with 3 different modes and marking 3 different sorts of work.

There can be no doubt that this has helped both schools and universities think much more seriously about accessibility - while (if done well) offering a positive alternative to deficit models of SEND. It also helps to get rid of the ‘fixing the learner’ mindset and focuses on possible barriers int he environment.

I also want to challenge the assumption that UDL seems to make that more choice = more inclusive. This flies in the face of most cognitive science I have ever encountered I feel, as it could increase extraneous load, distract from the central content and depressingly for already overwhelmed teachers, make classroom routines much more complicated.
However, the evidence base was small and highly heterogeneous, with many studies relying on one-group pre-test/post-test designs. The findings are therefore promising rather than conclusive.

This does not mean that captions, scaffolds, accessible texts or carefully selected representations are ineffective. He questioned whether evidence for these individual practices validates the wider UDL framework and the claims made for it.

For example, if the objective is to understand the causes of the First World War, pupils might demonstrate this understanding through several appropriate formats. If the objective is to construct a sustained historical argument in writing, a poster or podcast cannot simply replace the essay.
Inclusion does not mean providing a route around every difficulty. It means removing difficulties that are irrelevant to what pupils are supposed to learn.
